title: Fed Chair Warsh addresses Jackson Hole amid inflation and bond market turmoil
dek: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at the Jackson Hole economic conference on August 28 as inflation remains at 3.4%, well above the Fed's 2% target. His speech comes after bond market turbulence and criticism of his July communication. A Cleveland Fed official has called for rate increases.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh addresses Jackson Hole on August 28, 2026, three months into his tenure, as inflation sits at 3.4%, above the Fed's 2% target, and bond yields surge to decade-high levels.
bottom_line: Warsh's August 28 speech will test whether he can stabilize market confidence and signal a coherent inflation strategy without committing to the rate-increase timeline some officials and investors are demanding. Watch whether his statement moves bond yields and how the market interprets his stance on the pace of future policy adjustments.
body:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will address the Jackson Hole economic conference on August 28, 2026, at a moment when inflation remains elevated and the bond market has entered turmoil, according to NBC News. The setting presents a credibility test for a Fed chair three months into his tenure.
Inflation in July stood at 3.4 percent, per NBC News, well above the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target. Bond yields have surged to levels not seen in more than a decade, with experts citing Warsh's July news conference as a major contributor to the turmoil. According to Evercore analysts quoted by NBC News, "Warsh has ground to make up after his July press conference failed to articulate a coherent strategy for ensuring inflation returns to target and hit his credibility."
The Fed is widely expected to hold interest rates steady at its September policy meeting, according to NBC News. However, there is dissent within the Federal Open Market Committee. Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack voted to raise rates at the Fed's July meeting, though she was outvoted. Hammack stated, per NBC News, "I believe it's time to act. I think we've seen inflation above target for too long." She recounted visiting manufacturing workers in Erie, Pennsylvania, who told her they did not expect inflation to decline in the coming year, and she expressed concern about an "inflationary mindset starting to set in."
She also stressed that transparency is essential: "Transparency is critical for us to be able to explain to the public broadly how we're thinking about the economy and how we think things will progress."
Warsh has resisted pressure to provide forward guidance, or hints about the Fed's future policy moves. UBS economists noted, per NBC News, that "We do not expect forward guidance in Chairman Warsh's Jackson Hole speech" and that "a road map for the [Fed] funds rate for the remainder of the year has just not been his style." Warsh said last month he would use Jackson Hole to "frame the big questions" facing the Fed, according to NBC News.
The Treasury Department has intervened in bond markets by announcing plans to buy back at least $4 billion of long-dated government debt, according to NBC News.  Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of One Point BFG Wealth Partners, told NBC News, "The market is in the driver's seat" and "not even the Treasury Department can replace the market's ability to set long-term interest rates."
Hammack noted continuity within the Fed itself, stating per NBC News that "Things have been more similar than they've been different inside the [FOMC] meeting room," despite Warsh's shift away from forward guidance.
